```python
def count_rotation(arr):
    for i in range(len(arr) - 1):
        if arr[i] > arr[i + 1]:
            return i + 1
    return 0


assert count_rotation([3, 2, 1]) == 1
assert count_rotation([1, 2, 3]) == 0
assert count_rotation([3, 1, 2]) == 1
assert count_rotation([2, 3, 1]) == 2
assert count_rotation([4, 5, 1, 2, 3]) == 2
assert count_rotation([]) == 0
```

This scans for the first descent and returns the index just after it, or 0 if the array has none. For a rotated ascending array, that index is the position of the minimum, which is the rotation count. It runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra memory.

The GeeksforGeeks article gives an O(log n) binary-search solution for the minimum. I didn't use it because it returns 2 for `[3,2,1]` (the index of the minimum), which fails your assert.
